query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under simultaneous wear and corrosive attack, a stress‐induced formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline surface layer in high-entropy alloys creates a high density of active grain boundaries that both increases hardness (thus reducing mechanical degradation) and accelerates the formation and self-healing of a protective passive oxide film, thereby governing the alloy’s combined resistance to wear and corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a conventional coarse or moderately refined microstructure (e.g., a typical CoCrFeMnNi or AlCoCrFeNiMoTi alloy processed by standard melting or cladding) that exhibits a stable but not dynamically evolving passive film under static conditions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled pre-deformation or surface treatment (e.g., low-energy shot peening) to induce a stress-driven, dynamic nanostructural evolution (dynamic amorphization/nanocrystallization) in the near-surface region.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted in corrosive media (3.5 wt% NaCl solution) under simultaneous sliding wear conditions (using a reciprocating tribometer) at room temperature; parallel tests under inert (ultra-high vacuum) or non-oxidizing conditions serve as controls.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer with a high density of grain boundaries, which acts as both a mechanical barrier to wear and a fast diffusion network that promotes the rapid formation and repair of a protective oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding wear, mechanical stresses induce dynamic grain refinement and/or amorphization at the surface; the resultant nanostructure raises the local hardness (reducing wear) and increases grain boundary area, which serves as active sites for oxygen uptake. This accelerates the formation and re-passivation of protective oxide films, counteracting corrosion damage. In essence, the dynamic surface evolution couples mechanical strengthening and chemical self-healing.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline untreated alloy, the pre-treated alloy will demonstrate lower wear rates and reduced corrosion current densities during simultaneous tribocorrosion tests. The overall mass loss and electrochemical degradation will be significantly less in the sample with the induced nanostructured layer, while the passive film is observed to form more rapidly and heal wear-induced defects in real time.
generation.baseline: Untreated high-entropy alloy samples with conventional microstructures undergoing identical tribocorrosion conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic advantage should be most effective in oxidizing environments where passive film formation is possible; in inert or reducing atmospheres where oxide film formation is suppressed, the benefit of the nanostructured layer on corrosion resistance may not be realized despite enhanced wear resistance.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal builds by combining the dynamic amorphization and inverse Hall-Petch findings (PMC7311485::web::012::results_and_discussion) with evidence that a refined nanostructure supports stable passive film formation under tribocorrosion (PMC10456374::web::012::3_4_tribocorrosion_performance_after_ann). The new aspect is the hypothesis that the mechanically induced nanostructuring actively couples both improved hardness and accelerated passivation, which remains untested in combined degradation regimes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: (A) subject them to a controlled pre-deformation treatment (e.g., low-energy shot peening) to induce a near-surface nanocrystalline layer; (B) leave samples untreated (baseline). Conduct simultaneous wear-corrosion tests in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution using a reciprocating tribometer with real-time monitoring of wear track morphology and electrochemical potential. In addition, perform similar tests under inert (e.g., UHV) conditions.
measurements: Wear rate (mm³/(N·m)) and surface hardness via nanoindentation before and after the test.
Electrochemical measurements including corrosion current density and open-circuit potential (OCP) during sliding.
Microstructural characterization of the worn surfaces (e.g., TEM, SEM) to assess grain size and oxide film continuity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treated samples do not exhibit significantly lower wear rates and reduced corrosion current density compared to the untreated baseline under oxidizing conditions (or if the dynamic formation and self-healing of the oxide film cannot be verified in microstructural analyses), then the hypothesis that a stress-induced nanocrystalline surface promotes coupled wear and corrosion resistance is falsified. Additionally, if similar improvements occur under inert conditions where passivation is suppressed, the presumed coupling mechanism would be challenged.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.4. Tribocorrosion Performance after Annealing in Air Environment
cited_evidence.text: The influence of thermal shock on the tribocorrosion properties of AlCrTiZrMo HEA films is analyzed by monitoring the fluctuation of the OCP and COF of films in the coupled environment of friction and corrosion, as shown in Figure 10. The fluctuation of the OCP and COF of the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film and the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 400 °C, 600 °C and 800 °C for 1 h in air are monitored in real time. In the preparation stage, the samples were completely immersed in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution for 1 h to obtain a stable surface potential. The duration of the whole experiment is 50 min. During the no-load phase of 0–10 min, both the OCP and COF curves remain stable. During the 10–40 min loading stage, the appearance of the activation region causes the OCP curve to drop sharply, then fluctuate around a constant value. During the 40–50 min no-loading stage, the lack of load causes re-passivation within the wear track, and the OCP curve gradually returns to stability. Therefore, OCP can be used as a mixed potential to monitor the passivation state within the wear track [,,].

cited_evidence.text: The potentiodynamic polarization curves of AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx HEA coatings in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution are shown in Figure 7. All samples exhibit a passivation region, where the formation of the passive film prevents material exchange between the environment and the metal surface. Within this region, the current density increases at a reduced rate as the voltage rises. The polarization curves were fitted using the Tafel method, and the results for corrosion potential (Ecorr) and corrosion current density (icorr) are summarized in Table 3. Ecorr is a kinetic parameter that evaluates the corrosion sensitivity of metal materials, while icorr is commonly used to characterize the metal’s active dissolution and uniform corrosion rate [,]. S2 and S4 have the most positive and most negative Ecorr values, respectively, indicating the lowest and highest corrosion tendencies. When a small amount of B is added, the coating’s corrosion resistance improves, as evidenced by a 51.0% reduction in the icorr value of S2 compared to S1. AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

This work studied an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy that was manufactured using a laser-based consolidation additive manufacturing process. We showed that low friction and high wear resistance are achievable with bare high entropy alloys in inert environments. These characteristics are linked to the shear-induced formation of a highly refined, near-amorphous surface film that exhibits inverse Hall-Petch behavior. The detrimental role of environments, specifically those that result in oxidation, was mitigated by tribological testing in a UHV environment. A newly proposed amorphization model was used to accurately predict the grain size-dependent shear strength, and thus friction coefficient.
